title: Diwali Bonus and Gifts: Three Thresholds That Do Not Line Up
seoTitle: Diwali Bonus and Gift Tax Rules for Employers 2026
metaDescription: Diwali bonus and gift rules for 2026: statutory bonus under the Code on Wages, the new Rs 15,000 perquisite line, GST at Rs 50,000 and 194R at Rs 20,000.
excerpt: A festival envelope and a sweet box touch three separate rulebooks, and two of the numbers changed this year. What the Code on Wages now asks, where the gift perquisite line moved, why GST uses another figure, and the deadline three weeks after Diwali.
keywords: gst on diwali gifts to employees
gift to employees tax free limit 15000
section 194r tds on diwali gifts to dealers
itc on diwali gifts and hampers

faq.question: Is a Diwali bonus legally compulsory in India?
faq.answer: A festival gift is not, but statutory bonus can be. Under the Code on Wages an establishment with twenty or more people must pay eligible employees at least 8.33 percent of wages earned, or Rs 100 if higher, even in a loss-making year. A goodwill Diwali payment only counts towards that if you record it as such.

faq.question: What is the last date to pay statutory bonus for FY 2025-26?
faq.answer: Within eight months of the close of the accounting year, so 30 November 2026 for a year that ended on 31 March 2026. An extension needs an application to the appropriate Government and cannot run beyond two years in total. The bonus must now be credited to the employee's bank account rather than paid in cash.

faq.question: How much can I gift an employee tax-free this Diwali?
faq.answer: Gifts in kind are a nil perquisite where the employee's aggregate for the whole tax year stays below Rs 15,000, up from Rs 5,000 previously. Cash and anything cash-equivalent gets no such relief and is taxed as salary from the first rupee, so a cash envelope changes their TDS.

faq.question: Can I claim input tax credit on Diwali gifts and hampers?
faq.answer: No. Credit is blocked on goods disposed of by way of gift or free samples, so the GST you paid on the purchase becomes part of the cost. The October 2026 GST Council recommendation on easing this covered free samples only, not gifts, and has not been notified in any case.

faq.question: Do I need to deduct TDS on gifts to dealers and distributors?
faq.answer: Usually yes, once a recipient's gifts total Rs 20,000 or more in a financial year, at which point section 194R applies 10 percent to the whole value. Small individuals and HUFs below the turnover limits are outside it. Because tax cannot be withheld from a hamper, you either recover it or gross it up.

bodyHtml:
Lakshmi Puja falls on Sunday 8 November, and most owners will hand out an envelope and a sweet box without thinking of either as a tax event. Both are. A Diwali payment to staff touches the Code on Wages, the income-tax perquisite rules and, for a hamper, GST as well — three rulebooks with thresholds that do not line up.

Two of those numbers changed in 2026, so last year's practice is not a safe guide. Here is what each rulebook asks this season, and the deadline three weeks after Diwali that catches people out.

The Diwali bonus and the statutory bonus are not the same payment

Most festival envelopes are ex-gratia: goodwill, at whatever amount feels right. Statutory bonus is a separate, legally owed amount with its own formula and deadline. The two can be the same cheque, but only if you say so in writing.

An owner who pays a generous ex-gratia in November, then gets asked in March for statutory bonus, has no record that the November money was meant to discharge it — and may pay twice. If the festival payment is meant to cover statutory bonus, the payslip has to say so and name the accounting year. One line settles it.

Statutory bonus under the Code on Wages: who, how much, by when

The four labour codes came into force on 21 November 2025 and the Central Rules were notified on 8 May 2026, so the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 is no longer the governing law. Bonus now sits in Chapter IV of the Code on Wages, 2019. Much of the shape is familiar; not all.

QuestionPosition under the Code
Which establishmentsTwenty or more persons employed on any day in the accounting year
Which employeesThose who worked at least thirty days in that year
Minimum bonus8.33% of wages earned, or ₹100, whichever is higher — due even in a loss-making year
Maximum bonus20% of wages earned in the accounting year
DeadlineWithin eight months of the close of the accounting year
How it must be paidCredited to the employee's bank account

Three rows deserve a second look. The twenty-person test is a change: the 1965 Act covered every factory regardless of headcount, so a small factory once inside the net may now sit outside it. The bank-credit requirement is new — cash in an envelope no longer discharges the obligation. And the eight-month deadline has a date attached: for a year that closed on 31 March 2026, statutory bonus is due by 30 November 2026. Three weeks after Diwali, not three months.

It can be extended only on application to the appropriate Government, never beyond two years.

New businesses get a real concession. For the first five accounting years from the first sale or service rendered, bonus is payable only in a year the employer actually derives profit, with set-on and set-off switched off. Years six and seven phase it in; from the eighth, the full mechanism applies.

The wage ceiling nobody has notified yet

Here is the genuinely unsettled part, worth being plain about rather than filling with last year's figure. Under the Code, bonus applies to employees drawing wages up to a limit set by notification — and commentary through mid-2026 reported that no limit had been prescribed. The old ₹21,000 and ₹7,000 figures come from the 1965 Act and are not in the Code.

What the Code does say: where wages exceed the notified amount, bonus is still payable, calculated as if wages were that amount or the applicable minimum wage, whichever is higher. The ceiling caps the computation, not eligibility. State rules are also still landing and they differ, so ask your CA what applies in your state before computing anything. We covered the wider payroll effects in what the new labour codes change for payroll.

Gifts in kind to staff: the ₹15,000 line that moved this year

A sweet box, a dry-fruit hamper, a kettle, a gift voucher — all perquisites, tax-free only up to a threshold. That threshold went up this year.

Under the Income-tax Rules, 2026, which apply from tax year 2026-27 alongside the Income-tax Act, 2025, the perquisite value of gifts, vouchers or tokens given to an employee or their household is nil where the aggregate is below ₹15,000 in the tax year. The old limit was ₹5,000 — three times the headroom, which for most small employers puts an ordinary hamper comfortably clear.

Two details are easy to get wrong. The relief reads "below" the figure, so an aggregate landing exactly on ₹15,000 is outside it. And it is all-or-nothing on the year's total, not a deduction: on the cautious reading, once the aggregate reaches the threshold the whole value becomes the perquisite, not the slice above. Gifts to household members count towards the same total, as does anything given at Holi or a work anniversary. Add up the year, not the hamper.

Cash is different, and the difference is total

None of that headroom applies to money. A cash Diwali bonus, a bank transfer, or anything cash-equivalent is salary from the first rupee — it enters the salary estimate for the year and TDS is recomputed under section 392 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, which was section 192 under the old Act.

The consequence lands on the employee, in a month they are not expecting it. Someone below the taxable line all year can be pushed over it by one November payment, and the deduction appears in their next payslip with no explanation. Run it through a take-home salary calculator before you pay and tell them what to expect.

The GST threshold is a different number doing a different job

This is where owners most often conflate two rules. GST has its own line for employee gifts and it is ₹50,000, not ₹15,000. Employer and employee are related persons under GST, so a transfer without consideration would ordinarily be a deemed supply under Schedule I — except that gifts not exceeding ₹50,000 in a financial year are not a supply at all.

ThresholdWhich lawWhat it decides
₹15,000Income-tax Rules, 2026Whether the gift is a taxable perquisite for the employee
₹50,000GST, Schedule IWhether the gift is a deemed supply you must charge GST on
₹20,000Section 194R, income taxWhether you must deduct TDS on a gift to a dealer or client

So a ₹20,000 hamper to one employee is a taxable perquisite for them and no GST supply for you. The numbers are not alternatives — each is checked separately. Above ₹50,000 it gets contentious: whether GST applies to the whole value or only the excess is disputed, with the revenue taking the wider view. At that level, do not resolve it yourself.

One useful carve-out: a festive benefit forming part of the contractual terms of employment is treated as outside GST. Written into the appointment letter, an annual hamper stands on firmer ground than one handed out at discretion.

The input credit you have to let go

Whatever GST you paid buying the hampers, you almost certainly cannot claim. The law blocks input tax credit on goods disposed of by way of gift or free samples, so the tax becomes part of the cost.

Budget for it before you order. On dry-fruit boxes and most packaged gift lines at 5%, a ₹60,000 purchase carries roughly ₹3,000 of GST you will not recover; on an 18% item, about ₹9,150. Record the full invoice value in the expense tracker under a festival or staff-welfare category so the season's real cost stays visible. If you have already claimed the credit, it needs an ITC reversal — better made deliberately than found later.

The October 2026 GST Council meeting recommended easing the restriction for free samples. It did not extend that to gifts or hampers, and it has not been notified, so nothing changes this year.

Hampers to dealers and clients: Section 194R at ₹20,000

Gifts outside the payroll are the part small businesses most often miss. Where you give a benefit to a dealer, distributor, channel partner or client in the course of business, section 194R requires TDS at 10% of its value — 20% with no PAN on record. The threshold is ₹20,000 aggregate per recipient per financial year, and once crossed the deduction applies to the whole value.

Smaller businesses are carved out: an individual or HUF with previous-year turnover up to ₹1 crore in business, or gross receipts up to ₹50 lakh in a profession, is outside it. So are your own employees, and ordinary trade and cash discounts on a sale — it is benefits beyond the sale price that are caught.

The oddity is that a hamper cannot have tax withheld from it. The tax must be settled before the benefit is released, so you either recover the 10% from the recipient or bear it and gross the value up. Most firms bear it, putting the real cost of a ₹25,000 client gift closer to ₹27,800. And where 194R applied and nothing was deducted, 30% of the expenditure can be disallowed.

The gifts are generally deductible as business promotion or staff welfare where incurred wholly and exclusively for the business. Gifts to government officials are disallowed outright.

What to do this week

  • Decide whether the festival payment is ex-gratia or statutory bonus and write it on the payslip. If statutory, name the accounting year.
  • Put 30 November 2026 in the diary if your year closed on 31 March and you have twenty or more people. Accrue it now with a provision in the journal entry page.
  • Total each employee's gifts for the whole tax year, not just the hamper, and check it against the ₹15,000 line.
  • Recompute TDS before paying any cash bonus, and tell the employee what to expect.
  • Value every dealer and client gift and check each recipient against ₹20,000. Decide who bears the 194R tax.
  • Do not claim input credit on gift purchases — use a GST calculator to size the irrecoverable tax before approving the order.
  • Check what your state has notified — the wage ceiling and several procedural rules are set at state level.

None of this is tax advice

Thresholds and the state rules under the labour codes are all moving, and two figures here changed inside the last twelve months. The ₹15,000 perquisite limit is new enough that practice is still settling, and the bonus wage ceiling is unresolved pending notification. Treat this as a map of what to ask, not a position to file on — confirm your own case with your CA before you pay. If you would rather someone looked at your payroll and gift list, that is what our consultancy team is for.
